verses.text: So what can we say Abraham, our ancestor by human descent, gained?
If Abraham was made right by what he did, he could brag—but not before God.
What does Scripture say? ‘Abraham believed God, and God counted him as righteous.’
When someone works, their pay isn't a gift; it's what they're owed.
But when someone doesn't rely on their work and instead trusts God, who makes the ungodly right, that faith is counted as righteousness.
David says the same thing when he describes the blessing God gives apart from works:
‘Blessed are those whose lawless acts are forgiven and whose sins are covered.
Blessed is the person whose sin the Lord will never count against them.’
Is this blessing only for the circumcised, or also for the uncircumcised? We say Abraham's faith was counted as righteousness.
So when was it counted—after he was circumcised or before? Not after, but before.

He received circumcision as a sign and a seal of the righteousness that came through faith while he was still uncircumcised. This made him the father of all who believe without being circumcised, so righteousness could be counted to them too.
He is also the father of the circumcised who don't just have the mark, but follow the footsteps of the faith our father Abraham had before he was circumcised.
The promise to Abraham and his descendants that he would inherit the world didn't come through the law. It came through righteousness by faith.
If the heirs were those who rely on the law, faith would be pointless and the promise would be canceled.
The law brings judgment. Where there is no law, there is no breaking of the law either.

That's why the promise comes by faith: so it can be a gift of grace and be guaranteed to all Abraham's descendants—not only those who have the law, but also those who share Abraham's faith. He is the father of us all.
As Scripture says, ‘I have made you the father of many nations.’ Abraham trusted God, who gives life to the dead and calls into existence what doesn't exist.
When hope seemed gone, Abraham still trusted in hope, believing he would become the father of many nations, just as God had said: ‘Your descendants will be so numerous.’
His faith didn't weaken, even though he knew his body was as good as dead—he was about a hundred years old—and Sarah's womb was unable to bear children.
He didn't let unbelief make him doubt God's promise. Instead, his faith grew stronger, and he gave glory to God.
He was fully convinced that God was able to do what he had promised.
That is why his faith ‘was counted to him as righteousness.’
Those words weren't written only for Abraham,
but also for us. God will count us righteous too when we believe in the one who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead.
Jesus was handed over because of our trespasses and raised to make us right with God.
